scope: Non-atomic read-only live LINSTOR, Kubernetes, SeaweedFS, ClickHouse, Mimir and Loki observations; no retention, replication, or volume changes.
units: Decimal GB for physical and logical bytes; GiB for requested PVC sizes. Reported pool limits are sums of diskful LINSTOR volume definitions on each node, not reservations or actual used bytes.

compression_sample.sampling: 0.5% PostgreSQL page sample, then up to three objects per prefix/month; individual objects compressed in memory. Not byte-representative.

clickhouse_evidence.sample_window: 150 litellm_request GENERATION rows from 2026-08-15, selected with LIMIT rather than random sampling
clickhouse_evidence.sample_top_parameter: 127 of 150 rows had tools; tool values represented 75.81 MiB of the sampled model-parameter JSON.
clickhouse_evidence.sample_top_metadata: The attributes object occupied 78.66 MiB, including 78.25 MiB for llm.invocation_parameters (150-row bounded sample).
clickhouse_evidence.sample_tool_equal: All 127 rows with tools had the same serialized tool definitions after decoding model_parameters.tools and metadata.attributes.llm.invocation_parameters.tools.
clickhouse_evidence.sample_core_equal: All 100 sampled rows present in both events_full and events_core had identical model_parameters SHA-256; 94 had matching tool definitions.
clickhouse_evidence.view_definition: events_core_mv truncates input, output and each metadata value to 200 characters but copies model_parameters untruncated.
clickhouse_evidence.recent: All 52 chat rows from 2026-11-10 had model_parameters under 1,000 bytes; combined model_parameters length was 134 bytes at the time of the query.
clickhouse_evidence.limits: Samples establish a duplication mechanism, not corpus-wide equality or safely reclaimable compressed bytes. Model parameters may be used by the Langfuse UI, API, filters and migrations; verify consumers and lossless historical coverage before altering stored values.
clickhouse_evidence.codec: system.parts reports LZ4 as the default codec on all active events_full and events_core parts. Input/output on events_full explicitly use ZSTD(3); model_parameters and metadata_values have no explicit column codec. Changing a codec does not instantly recompress existing parts.

options.title: Archive and expire old Langfuse ingestion objects
options.confidence: Measured age inventory; reclaim and archive overhead unmeasured
options.risk: Raw-only historical information; verify archive and replay before expiry.
options.detail: The 30-day cutoff covers 420.792 GB logical. Two Seaweed copies give an approximate 841.6 GB upper bound before archive costs, vacuum and discard. Seaweed compresses some underlying chunks, so actual physical reclaim can be substantially smaller than twice the S3 logical size. Objects older than 90 days total 75.688 GB logical. Keep media and exports outside any raw-event lifecycle.

options.title: Rebuild ClickHouse claims at 300 GiB
options.gain: 215 GB limit on each of two nodes
options.confidence: Measured 500-GiB claims; 116 GB used per filesystem
options.risk: New smaller PVCs and full replica catch-up are needed; verify Keeper, schema, data and consumers. Old Retain volumes need separate recovery-gated retirement.
options.detail: This lowers claim limits only after the old backing volumes are retired, not the current data bytes. Kubernetes cannot shrink the existing PVCs. With hard node anti-affinity, preserve both original hosts and two active replicas by using 103711 as a temporary third copy, then replacing each original replica in turn: 2→3→2→3→2→3→2. This requires three new PVCs/transfers and has not been rehearsed. It is an alternative to removing a ClickHouse replica.

options.title: Recreate the smaller Seaweed claims within their budgets
options.confidence: Calculated from live allocation and definition sizes
options.risk: Evacuate and rebuild one node at a time; verify replication and headroom throughout.
options.detail: Illustrative targets: 1,180 GiB on 103656 and 1,290 GiB on 103711, down from 1,700 GiB each. With the 300-GiB ClickHouse resize and GitLab spike retirement, these targets fit a 10% pool reserve. GitLab is active and migration-related; if retained, choose smaller Seaweed targets or another offset.

options.title: Benchmark compression and historical tool-definition deduplication
options.confidence: Sampled exact duplication; corpus and consumer coverage unproven
options.risk: Preserve tool definitions, lookup/filter behavior, backups and schema migration compatibility.
options.detail: The full and core model-parameter columns total 35.05 GB compressed per replica; full metadata adds 22.81 GB per replica. These are footprints, not additive reclaim estimates. A sampled subset stores identical tool definitions in both metadata and parameters; the core materialized view also duplicates parameters. Benchmark and prove coverage before rewriting anything. Existing parts use LZ4 by default for parameters and metadata; benchmark ZSTD before considering a controlled rewrite, and verify that Langfuse migrations preserve any codec change.

options.title: Use one copy for the Zot pull-through cache
options.confidence: 100-GiB claim and ~3.72 GiB filesystem use; observed active client traffic
options.risk: A node failure interrupts cache service and dependent image pulls until recovery.
options.detail: Keep the copy on 102453 and replace the replicated claim with a single-copy claim; the current 103711 replica accounts for this estimated reduction. Zot is actively serving manifest and blob requests, so confirm upstream refill and egress behavior before accepting the loss of replica failover.

options.title: Use one copy for the Attic cache
options.risk: A failed node can lose cached artifacts; first prove upstream availability or rebuilds.
options.detail: Keep the 102453 copy and remove the 103656 copy after a verified migration. Do not assume every cached artifact is reproducible.

options.title: Run a single ClickHouse replica
options.risk: No replica failover and a node failure can lose trace history; independently test recovery first.
options.detail: Alternative to right-sizing both replicas, not an additional saving. Keep the replica on 102453; confirm Keeper and application behavior.

options.title: Trim source-less HTTP flow metrics or shorten Mimir retention
options.gain: ~12% of current series; or ~200 GB physical above 90 days
options.gain_type: Future series or historical upper bound
options.confidence: Point-in-time series count; all block metadata and live S3 listing
options.risk: The filter loses HTTP counts for destinations without a source; 90-day retention loses all older metric history.
options.detail: 133,686 source-less L7 HTTP flow series are 12.5% of 1,073,249 current series; all Hubble flow series are 27.1%. Filtering affects future ingestion, not existing blocks, and compressed-byte savings are unmeasured. Hubble historical network attribution was deliberately enabled: audit ad-hoc use and preserve useful flow/drop metrics. Alternatively, blocks older than 90 days hold 100.24 GB logical (~200 GB with two Seaweed copies), before compaction and discard; the 365-day setting currently contains only about 161 days of data.

options.title: Investigate repetitive Talos audit events
options.gain: ~25–36 GB physical per 30 days: broad scenario only
options.confidence: Four five-minute byte/compression windows and nine bounded event samples
options.risk: Audit records preserve security evidence. Do not suppress all denials or infer that every SELinux decision is permissive.
options.detail: In a 3,000-AVC sample, all had permissive=1 and 2,943 involved unlabeled DRBD paths. Correlated fragments represented 86.4% of bytes in nine 1,000-line audit samples (18–100% per window). Investigate the SELinux labeling/policy cause and any narrowly scoped noise reduction first. The 25–36 GB scenario extrapolates removal of ALL auditd using 30-day indexed raw volume, sampled audit share and Talos compression, then doubles for Seaweed; it is not measured reclaim and targeted filtering would save less. Existing records cannot be selected by service-level retention because their streams lack that label.

options.title: Retire the GitLab spike only if its migration role ends
options.confidence: PVC sizes and active workload verified
options.risk: The spike is running and participates in the Forgejo-to-GitLab plan. Preserve the planned migration and any unique data.
options.detail: Three Gitaly 50-GiB claims plus two Valkey 5-GiB claims. This is conditional, not a recommendation to remove an active migration dependency.

sources.label: Langfuse S3 evidence and retention issue
Loki v3.6.11: TSDB indexes approximate uncompressed chunk bytes

observability.sampling_note: Mimir block age groups use maxTime of all 171 block metadata records and the file sizes on the filer, validated against a 963-object S3 listing. Blocks straddling a cutoff are included on the newer side. Mimir active-series counts are point-in-time estimates, not compressed bytes. Loki indexed byte estimates can include chunks overlapping interval boundaries, exclude streams without job, and are not physical bytes. Four five-minute windows estimate the audit share and chunk compression; nine 1,000-line node/time samples correlate audit fragments; neither is byte-weighted across the month. Four short KSM chunk samples estimate compression. No individual log lines or credentials were saved.

questions.question: Is Langfuse S3 data compressed across objects?
questions.answer: Langfuse uploads plain JSON. SeaweedFS compresses some underlying chunks with gzip level 1; compression is per chunk, not across objects.
details: All 36 sampled S3 responses had JSON content type, no Content-Encoding and plain-JSON prefixes; 35 were fully read and parsed. In the complete set of 43 OTEL objects listed for November 10 at inspection time, each had one chunk; 40 were stored compressed and three were not. Together their 17,068,868 S3-body bytes occupied 5,109,775 bytes of chunk bodies, excluding overhead and copies.

All 12 sampled historical legacy objects and 12 sampled historical OTEL objects had uncompressed chunk metadata. These bounded samples are not a bucket-wide census. Media and exports were empty, so their formats were not checked.

The 40 compressed chunks were independently decoded as gzip/DEFLATE. SeaweedFS 4.53 uses Go gzip BestSpeed (level 1) and keeps compressed output when it is sufficiently smaller; larger objects may span separate chunks. S3 transparently returns decompressed JSON. The earlier zstd/gzip chart compares fetched bodies and is not a measurement of incremental savings over current disk use. An OTEL JSON object contains a resource-spans batch, so repetitions inside a chunk can compress together, but no compression dictionary crosses object boundaries.

questions.question: Does SeaweedFS S3 and its operator support compression?
questions.answer: Yes: SeaweedFS automatically gzip-compresses eligible S3 upload chunks. Our operator-managed deployment already uses that behavior.
details: In SeaweedFS 4.53, the S3 uploader passes the Content-Type to its chunk uploader. Recognized types such as application/json are eligible; the compressed chunk is kept only if it is smaller than 90% of the original. Each chunk is compressed independently with gzip/DEFLATE at Go BestSpeed (level 1). S3 transparently returns the original object.

The operator chart 0.1.42 / controller 1.0.39 has no dedicated compression enable, algorithm, level, MIME-list or threshold setting. It exposes generic arguments and environment variables, but these do not create a missing native knob. It does expose filer.maxMB; ours is unset, so the S3 chunk size defaults to 4 MiB.

This applies to eligible new writes and does not retroactively compress old objects. Changing storage of old data would require an independently verified rewrite or migration; physical reclaim would also depend on compaction. Client-provided S3 Content-Encoding is separate from transparent storage compression.

questions.question: Is the Zot pull-through cache actively used?
questions.answer: Yes: clients actively request manifests and image blobs from Zot. The available metrics cannot yet establish a cache-hit percentage or total bandwidth saved.
details: For the 24 hours ending 2026-11-10 22:02:23 UTC, Loki recorded 1,782 successful client manifest GETs and about 105.7 GB of successful blob response bodies. Clients included containerd, Docker and BuildKit. Response bytes can include upstream misses and repeat transfers; they are not measured bytes saved.

A nearby 24-hour Prometheus window showed about 679.5 outer-cluster kubelet pull operations, while Zot counted about 3,949.7 manifest reads, including internal reads and HEAD requests. These have different units and coverage. Nested K3s, Docker and BuildBuddy consumers are not captured by the outer kubelet denominator, so do not divide the values to infer a hit rate.

The cache filesystem used about 3.72 GiB of its 100-GiB claim at inspection. The Grafana dashboard separates client requests, blob bytes, kubelet calls, cache size and GC; a universal all-pulls denominator requires additional runtime/source telemetry.

questions.question: Does Zot have a retention policy?
questions.answer: Yes. GC is enabled with a 24-hour interval, and a policy retains recently used tags per repository.
details: For every repository, tags are kept if pulled within 720 hours (30 days) OR among the 20 most recently pulled. Other tags are eligible for removal. Unreferenced untagged manifests are eligible after the 24-hour retention delay; orphan blobs use gcDelay of one hour. Referenced multi-architecture children are preserved; there is no hard byte cap, and the top 20 tags can remain indefinitely.

The process is active: over the sampled 24-hour window the GC counters increased by about 139 deleted blobs and 59 deleted manifests. Eleven successful repository jobs appeared in one daily sweep; the GC run counter is per repository, not eleven global sweeps.

questions.question: Can we shrink the existing ClickHouse PVCs?
questions.answer: Kubernetes does not support shrinking a PVC in place. Use smaller replacement volumes; four simultaneous replicas are unnecessary.
details: The two existing 500-GiB replicas use about 116 GB each. Replacing them with 300-GiB claims would reduce declared limits by about 215 GB per replica only after the old backing resources are actually retired; it does not immediately free 200 GiB of data per replica.

Hard node anti-affinity permits at most three replicas on the three HDD hosts. To end on both original hosts while keeping two running replicas, add a temporary replica on 103711, replace the old replica on 103656, replace the old replica on 102453, then retire the temporary one. The active replica count is 2→3→2→3→2→3→2: three new PVCs and transfers, at most three active replicas.

Only two new replicas would finish on 103711 and one original host. Alternatively, replacing one original replica at a time without the temporary third copy would leave only one copy during each rebuild, reducing fault tolerance.

This is a proposed sequence, not a rehearsed migration. A 300-GiB claim on 103711 passed read-only capacity checks, but temporarily raises its already-overcommitted limits. Verify Keeper quorum, schema and view definitions, replication catch-up and consumer behavior before removing each old copy. Retain leaves old volumes behind; their removal is a separate recovery-gated step. LINSTOR supports some lower-level shrinking, but that is not a supported Kubernetes PVC shrink path. If both old volumes and the temporary volume are retained through the rotation, the five volume limits peak at 1,900 GiB; physical allocation is a separate measure.
